source.title: On the SDEs and Scaling Rules for Adaptive Gradient Algorithms
source.authors: Sadhika Malladi; Kaifeng Lyu; Abhishek Panigrahi; Sanjeev Arora

record.file_problem: The supplied text contains the paper, appendices, and checklist. Some figure content is flattened, but the text describes the relevant comparisons.
record.tranche_reason: The study compares held-out performance across batch sizes using a different recipe: it adjusts adaptive optimizer hyperparameters according to a square-root scaling rule and also compares linear scaling. These results bear on V5’s batch-size condition.
record.gate_note: The study reports results for adaptive optimizers with scaled hyperparameters and compares a linear-scaling recipe on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet. It does not test the unadjusted large-batch penalty as a standalone comparison. The scaling ablations’ train and validation curves are described as comparisons; only reported validation/test-performance outcomes are included below.
record.test_reason: The study measures held-out performance across batch sizes with adapted Adam and RMSprop recipes. Fixed epoch budgets in the vision experiments directly test V5's qualification that recipe changes can reduce the large-batch penalty; ImageNet linear-scaling experiments also demonstrate recipe-dependent failure.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors derive SDE approximations and square-root scaling rules for RMSprop and Adam, and conclude that experiments approximately preserve measured trajectories and held-out performance across batch sizes. Their theorems do not directly cover the time-varying schedules used experimentally. Empirical preservation allows small residual accuracy gaps.
record.recipe_differences: The study derives and evaluates SDE-based square-root scaling for RMSprop and Adam, adjusting learning rates and adaptive hyperparameters as batch size changes. Its experiments compare this with alternative partial and linear scaling rules; it does not test random-label memorization or the original batch-size intervention without adaptation.
record.method_sensitivity: The outcome varies with the scaling rule: scaling all adaptive hyperparameters performed best in the CIFAR-10 ablation, linear scaling was comparable on CIFAR-10, and linear scaling reduced ImageNet validation performance. Epsilon settings and dataset also vary across reported experiments.

fits_no_version.finding: Linear and square-root scaling yield comparable CIFAR-10 validation accuracy at large batches.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Different adaptive-optimizer scaling recipes can reach similar held-out accuracy despite differing training trajectories.

record.code_released: Vision experiment code included in supplementary material; NLP experiments use https://github.com/princeton-nlp/DinkyTrain
record.problems: The theoretical results assume well-behaved losses and gradient noise satisfying bounded-moment and low-skewness conditions; the authors identify heavy-tailed gradient noise as a limitation. Experimental uncertainty is incompletely reported: the checklist says error bars were not included for all experiments. Several performance comparisons are stated as maximum gaps or qualitative similarities rather than per-batch values.
record.rows_left_out: The paper reports downstream GLUE scores for RoBERTa models pretrained at different batch sizes in Table 1, with separate task metrics and batch-size entries. These task-by-task results are not extracted as rows because they would exceed the row budget when expanded by task and batch-size condition; the accompanying prose says the models achieve very similar downstream performance. Other plotted trajectory comparisons and SVAG approximation results were left out because they concern optimization-trajectory matching rather than the batch-size held-out-performance claim.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and its contrast with natural-label held-out accuracy.
Width sweeps beyond the interpolation threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected architectures and local connectivity.
Adaptive versus SGD held-out performance under limited or broader tuning.

A fully unadapted batch-size sweep; longer-training remedies; separate normalization and regularization interventions. Language experiments do not establish matched completed epoch budgets for every run.
Dropout interventions and removal of dropout with weight decay.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its correlation with generalization gaps.
Removing memorized examples versus random removals.

missing.what: The CIFAR-10 held-out-performance ablation comparing full square-root scaling against scaling only subsets of the adaptive hyperparameters. The authors state that full scaling consistently performs best, with scaling learning rate, epsilon and beta1 closest. These results establish recipe dependence but are not captured by R9's linear-rule comparison.
missing.locator: Appendix I.1 and Figure 24, batches 2048, 4096, 8192 and 16384

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source for any listed version. Row states describe the large-batch penalty; an absent penalty under an adapted recipe can support V5's explicit adaptation qualification. GLUE results are already declared in rows_left_out and therefore are not listed as missing.

versions.untested_parts: Convolutional versus fully connected image models.

The unadapted large-batch penalty is not isolated across all settings; the paper focuses on adapted hyperparameters and does not test every normalization or regularization change named in the version.

rows.subject: RoBERTa-large
rows.operation_detail: Pretrained at different batch sizes, scaling Adam hyperparameters by the proposed rule.
rows.value: Validation log perplexity of 2.1 ± 0.1 for batch size 1024, 2048, 4096 and 8192; batch size 256 follows the same behavior during its 48-hour trajectory.

rows.note: The paper describes the train and validation log perplexities as close across batch sizes.
rows.check: The authors report matching validation trajectories, rather than an observed large-batch penalty. The ±0.1 is a reported performance range, not an identified statistical uncertainty estimate. Runs have a 48-hour cap, and batch 256 does not reach the same trajectory endpoint; exclude it from matched final-performance comparisons.

rows.subject: ResNet-50
rows.operation_detail: Compared the proposed square-root rule with a linear rule scaling η, 1 − β1, and 1 − β2 by the batch-size factor while keeping ϵ fixed.
rows.value: The linear scaling rule seems to perform as well as the proposed square-root scaling rule in terms of validation accuracies.
rows.locator: Appendix I.2, Figures 24–25 and accompanying text
rows.note: The authors qualify that the square-root rule tracks the smaller-batch training trajectory better; CIFAR-10 may be simple enough for different rules to work well.
rows.check: As extracted, this measures linear versus square-root recipe performance at large batches, not large versus small batches. It should not independently count as a batch-size-effect row. Figure 25 contains a batch-256 control, but the extracted value gives no explicit held-out difference from that control.

rows.subject: ResNet-50
rows.operation_detail: Compared a linear rule scaling η, 1 − β1, and 1 − β2 by the batch-size factor, leaving ϵ fixed, with the proposed square-root rule.
rows.value: The authors observe a decrease in performance at larger batch size in comparison to a model trained with square-root scaling.
rows.locator: Appendix I.2, Figure 26 and accompanying text
rows.note: The decrease is described qualitatively; no numerical accuracy difference is stated.
rows.check: The effect is a large-batch penalty, not its reversal. Record the batch-256 linear-rule run as the batch-size baseline, with batches 1024, 4096 and 16384 as interventions; square-root scaling is an additional recipe comparator. Appendix I.2 explicitly reports a large validation-accuracy drop at larger batches under the same 90-epoch budget.
